title: My workers or ours? How labor sharing shapes hiring in urban firm clusters: Guest post by Zachary Kuloszewski

My workers or ours? How labor sharing shapes hiring in urban firm clusters: Guest post by Zachary Kuloszewski

Development Impact Guest Blogger

November 20, 2026

This page in:

English

This is the 11th in this year’s series of posts by PhD students on the job market.
“Who do you work for?” usually has a simple answer: a business, a shop owner, or a family member exclusively hires a worker for an agreed-upon duration. But if you ask this question in a busy workshop, you may hear the names of many different firms or owners. In my job market paper, I break down why the answer to this question can be a bit more complicated in dense, informal labor markets.
Small, informal firms, which employ the majority of workers in sub-Saharan Africa, face many challenges hiring and maintaining an appropriately sized workforce. Worker ability is hard to judge before a worker is on the job, so vetting a new hire is slow and costly. Demand from consumers can vary widely week to week. Firms confronting both issues face the difficult choice of carrying idle labor during slow periods or being left unprepared for peaks in demand. In high-income countries, firms turn to formal temporary agencies. What do firms do in the absence of these formal intermediaries?
In urban Uganda, I survey over 500 firms and 1,000 of their workers to show that firms rely on labor sharing, borrowing workers directly from their competitors, to cope with both high hiring costs and shifting demand. By offering on-demand workers who come pre-verified by a neighboring firm, labor sharing provides flexible capacity, allowing hiring managers to reach across the firm boundary and meet their spikes in demand without sacrificing quality. In effect, skilled workers have a “home firm” but are frequently reallocated to others nearby. In the paper, I combine detailed hiring data with stated choice experiments to estimate an equilibrium model investigating how labor sharing changes hiring and the impacts of labor market policies.
What is labor sharing?
Labor sharing is a distinctive kind of exchange used for temporary work, organized through firm-to-firm relationships rather than an open market. These exchanges have a common structure; they are reciprocal, uncompensated, and owner-coordinated. When one firm receives a large order, the owner requests workers from other same-industry firms nearby, with the borrowing firm paying the shared worker’s wages for the duration of the job, which is often less than a week.
Labor sharing is common and frequently used in the carpentry and metalworking sectors of Kampala, with 80% of firms reporting borrowing a worker from a competitor, and the average sharing firm borrowing or lending about once every ten days. Beyond Uganda, it has been qualitatively documented in Tanzania and Indonesia, where urban markets also feature dense firm clusters. Thus, questions of its structure and impact are important to understanding how small firms (collectively) function in low-income markets.
Labor sharing carries a quality signal and is available on demand
As in many low-income labor markets, workers lack credible signals of quality or skill. Permanent hiring is slow, taking over 4 days to screen a new worker. To examine labor sharing’s role in addressing this screening friction, I elicit firm beliefs about worker characteristics by asking firm owners about worker quality, screening time, and supervision needs. Owners expect 6.3 of 10 hires through labor sharing to make sellable products without further training, higher than any other hiring channel, including social network referrals (p<0.001).  Owners report the least time to screen new shared workers and the fewest hours of supervision, consistent with the idea that borrowing workers avoids high hiring costs, cited by 58% as an advantage of sharing.
Shared workers are also valuable because they are a timely response to short-term, firm-specific demand shocks, which come in the form of large orders. A busy month brings in five times the revenue of a slow month, and over half of owners report that their first response to unexpected demand spikes is to hire via labor sharing.
I combine these market features in the design of stated choice experiments where firms face hypothetical demand shocks and choose between potential extra hires to add to their staff. The experiments show how much firms value specific worker attributes [Figure 1]. I find firms are willing to pay a wage premium of roughly 53,000 Ugandan shillings per week ($14) for a shared worker over a similar walk-in worker. This premium is equivalent to about five years of industry experience, or a third of the median weekly wage.
Figure 1

 
In stated choice experiments for workers, I measure worker preferences by presenting hypothetical job offers varying the worker’s personal connection to a new firm, along with other attributes. I find that workers value opportunities through labor sharing about the same as other types of referrals, but more than jobs at firms where they have no prior connection. The worker choice experiments importantly show that workers positively value being lent out through labor sharing despite the implicit uncertainty or adjustment costs. Over 90% of workers are paid piece rate and earn little in slow periods, so being shared acts as a form of earnings insurance across firms and improves worker capacity utilization.
What sharing does to the labor market
Firms and workers both make staffing and employment decisions internalizing the presence of labor sharing as an additional hiring margin. Before knowing their demand from consumers, firms face a choice to hire now or borrow later. Borrowing brings assurances of skill for an additional cost, such as future lending obligations, which I measure in total from the choice experiments above. I formalize these trade-offs in an equilibrium model of hiring where workers choose firms based on wages and amenities (including the ability to be shared), and firms hire under uncertainty about consumer demand and worker skill.  
Compared to an economy where firms hire only via walk-ins and referrals, the economy with labor sharing creates 7.0% more surplus, benefiting skilled workers and firms. This economy also supports more, smaller firms, as it reduces the carrying costs of slack labor. The gains are driven by improved allocation of workers across demand states [Figure 2, top panel]. When firms can share, the fraction of skilled-worker time spent at busy firms doubles, leading to increased profits for firms and higher earnings for shared workers.
However, labor sharing changes who hires and holds permanent workers. With labor sharing, permanent jobs shift toward lower-productivity firms [Figure 2, bottom panel]. In effect, the ability to share separates hiring costs from worker utilization. Lower-productivity firms screen and hire workers, then lend them out to higher-productivity firms, which are more likely to meet their labor demand by borrowing than by permanently hiring. In the model, top-tercile firms use 46% of busy-week skilled work and produce over half of the economy’s output, while holding only 29% of permanent skilled jobs.
Figure 2

Lessons for policy
One of the key roles of the firm in these markets is to match customer orders to the right workers. Labor sharing is a market adaptation which helps firms collectively achieve this goal, but it also provides a degree of skill verification. So, it may interact with commonly implemented skill policies, such as certification or training. In my model:
Certification makes hiring skilled workers through walk-ins or referrals comparatively cheaper and concentrates gains among low-productivity lending firms (+4% profits) at the expense of high-productivity borrowers (-17%).
Training increases the supply of skilled labor and enables high-productivity firms to hire permanently instead of relying on borrowing, leading these firms to grow.
Taken together, these findings suggest existing informal institutions can determine who gains from labor market policy. Policymakers seeking to improve firm efficiency and worker outcomes in low-income markets should account for firm-to-firm interactions when considering and designing policy tools.
Zachary Kuloszewski is a Ph.D. candidate in Economics at the University of Chicago. On Twitter/X: @ZachKulos.
